transcription.text: Hello, everyone, and thank you for coming back after the lunch break.
We might begin again.
This afternoon we have two panel sessions.
One focusing on consumers, repairers and the right to repair.
And this afternoon we'll be looking more at product stewardship, which will be a great
panel as well.
So just to kick off, I'd like to introduce our panellists.
We have Tim Hicks, and I think you might have heard from Kyle this morning that Tim Hicks
had a little bit of an issue with Toshiba, and that's why Tim is here today to have a
little chat about his experience.
We also have online Lesley Yates from the Australian Automotive Parts Association, AAAA.
And we also have Guido, who's joining today.
And we have Erin from CHOICE.
Just getting a little bit of feedback.
Sorry, everyone.
Is that okay?
So Karen, I think Karen and Guido were just waiting to join our other panellists for this
particular session.
Just to kick off, I thought we might start off with Tim and get Tim to share a little
bit of his experience with your repair story.
Yeah, absolutely.
So hello, everyone.
This is extremely surreal.
So my name's Tim Hicks.
My story for coming here today is basically back in 2009, 2010, I was working for a small
computer repair shop down the coast.
It was my first real job.
One of the things that we kept seeing more and more was people needing repairs to their
laptops that they bought.
You know, lots of things can go wrong with laptops.
Leave them on the car, they disappear, the screen breaks.
You break the power points in them as well, making them very hard to recharge.
A challenge that we came up with again and again was that there was no real source of
information on repairing these laptops.
Obviously, a desktop computer is very easy to repair.
It's a set of standard parts.
It's relatively standard to work in them.
But laptops, there was nothing.
So I started on a bit of a search.
I found as many laptop service manuals as I could on the internet, just from other people's
sites who'd posted two or three from whatever they'd been able to find.
My website quickly became what I believe to be the biggest...
I'm not sure if that was me.
Sorry.
Right.
So my site became what I believe to be the biggest...
I swear that's not for dramatic effect.
Became the biggest repository of laptop service manuals anywhere on the internet.
That was working really, really well for a few years, until 2012.
I'd moved on to a different job by then, but I'd maintained the website.
And so she just sent me a fairly nasty takedown request.
They claimed that I had breached their copyright in reproducing their service manuals, and
long story short, I ended up taking them down.
I didn't want to get into a massive legal fight with a multi-million dollar international
company.
That's not my sort of thing.
So yeah, unfortunately I had to take them down.
As my site is at the moment, I still have manuals available from other brands.
No other brand has actually come to me and told me to take them down, which is interesting
because they must all be aware of it by now.
I feel like my site is sort of operating in a sort of grey area of tacit approval.
But as I said, no one else has...
I haven't had a takedown request from anywhere else.
It kind of actually fizzled out in the end, because I had a little bit of media interest
after everything happened.
Kyle wrote a lovely article about me in Wired, which has been a fantastic fact to use in
trivia.
Yeah, I do actually have a little bit of an update on this.
A couple of years ago, Toshiba actually sold their stake in their own laptop business to,
I believe it was Sharp Electronics.
So Toshiba actually no longer make and sell their own laptops.
The satellite brand of laptops is now entirely a different brand, it's no longer Toshiba.
I can't help but feel a little bit of responsibility for that.
So yeah, that is basically my story, that's why I'm here.
Thank you, Tim.
Now we can see all panel members along with Tim.
Erin, hi, from Choice.
I might turn to you now, just to share some of Choice's insight as to repairability in
consumer goods, perhaps.
I'd be really happy to.
And thank you for bringing us together today, Leanne.
You're welcome.
I'm really excited to have this conversation.
Are you getting a bit of feedback there?
No, you're perfect.
Oh, no worries then.
Look, I want to say, to start out with, that right to repair is a really big debate.
There are a lot of different problems that consumers face, but actually at the core of
it is large multinational companies throwing their weight around.
And it ties really neatly to the experience that Tim's had.
And these are companies that are looking to dominate markets.
So I want to make three really brief comments to start today.
The first is that consumer demand is there.
Consumers want products that last.
And as an independent, not-for-profit consumer group, we regularly poll consumers, we try
to get an understanding of what they want.
And what we see consistently is that people want things that are durable and repairable.
We did a survey earlier this year, and 85% of people told us they're buying things that
last a long time is really important.
73% said repairability is important.
So demand's there, but the market isn't fully responding.
And I think that helps us think about our policy solutions.
How do we get markets, and particularly big manufacturers, to meet what consumers want?
I really appreciated the point that Minister Rattenbury made earlier in the day, that we
need to start thinking about more than end-of-the-line solutions.
And that was the second thing I'd love to say.
I'm hopeful that we can lift the quality of products.
One way we need to think about doing that is by starting with the information at point
of sale.
At Choice, we've got a lot of experience with this.
When you think about what we need, what we need is a ranking system for the quality of
products.
So something that can easily tell us how long something will last, and how easy will it
be to fix if it breaks.
We've been doing this essentially for 60 years, but we don't want this information to stay
on the Choice website.
It would be ideal if people had this at the point of sale, when you're going to buy something.
We want to work towards something along the lines of a mandatory labelling scheme.
Something where you can quickly glance at a product and just see, you know, is it any
good?
Is it better than the one next to it?
And we know when these schemes exist, that companies and manufacturers compete on these
factors.
You can see it in the Australian market right now with the water and energy labelling scheme.
The best example that we love to point to is dishwashers.
A long time ago, dishwashers weren't very water-efficient.
I think a lot of households got into that habit of hand-washing their dishes.
I think some people still do that, on the assumption that it uses less water.
But now, actually, dishwashers in Australia are so water-efficient, you're better off
using those machines.
So if you can create a great, simple system that starts to rank products on these factors,
companies will compete.
Standards will lift.
This is going to be one of the first interventions we make.
There are other ways to lift durability, design standards, bans on poor quality, like a ban
on planned obsolescence.
I want all of those solutions.
But if we think where we can start, it's public, consistent, standardised ranking.
And then thinking more about those end-of-the-line solutions.
How do we help people when something breaks?
I think a lot of this is stopping the blockers that businesses create when you want to get
a refund, a replacement or a repair.
Such businesses use their power to make this process difficult.
And I've really appreciated that the Productivity Commission draft report has acknowledged really
clearly that we've got great rights under the Australian Consumer Law.
But businesses aren't always upfront about them, or in the experience of a lot of Choice
members, can actively ignore them, or just tell you that they may not apply, when they
clearly do.
Now, the Productivity Commission has put forward that idea of the ACCC providing guidance on
product durability.
It's great, but we're really hopeful for more.
We'd love to see interventions that will mean that companies stop exploiting the lack of
consumer knowledge around consumer guarantees, that they have to proactively provide this
information about how long a product will last and what your rights are.
And we're also really pleased to see that Productivity Commission put forward that idea
of a super complaints power.
This is also one of those interventions that will really help us challenge the power of
big manufacturers.
What it is, is the ability for groups that act in the consumer or the public interest
to raise a complaint that has to be publicly responded to by a regulator.
It's essentially people power with legal oomph.
If we had this, I know I've got a short list of issues I'd love to put up for a super complaint,
and I think every panel member here today would have their own list of issues as well.
I think that tells me this is a power we need to make happen.
It's something that we could really use very quickly to help act against companies that
repeatedly fail to offer repairs and help their customers.
That's what I wanted to say in opening.
I'm really excited for the conversation.
Thanks so much, Erin.
And the aim of today is really just to have a snapshot from each of these present presenters
today and then open it up for a more engaging discussion around some of the issues that
are raised.
Guido, you're a repair advocate and the new general manager of Revolve Recycle.
Would you like to talk to us about your repair experiences?
I think you're on mute.
Lesley, I'll just invite you to jump in and Guido can work out his tech, if that's okay.
This is Lesley Yates, as I mentioned before, from the AAAA, and she's very heavily involved
in managing the data sharing journey with the AAAA.
Welcome, Lesley.
Thanks, Leanne, and hello to everyone there and my fellow panellists.
I thought I'd talk a little today about the activities that we're undertaking in supporting
consumer awareness, because I know how frustrated we all are about the confusion between the
manufacturer's warranty and a consumer's statutory rights.
We had several conversations with government and with the AACC in particular about the
confusion that reigns and how consumers who aren't aware of their rights are unlikely
to be able to achieve what are their statutory rights.
And we know from the AACC inquiries that manufacturers are relying upon the manufacturer's warranty
as their first conversation for repair, refund or replace, rather than a consumer's statutory
guarantee.
So, I think the day we decided to provide information and literature to our members
to support consumer choice was a real kind of growing up for us.
We decided that a consumer that is aware of their rights were more likely to be one of
our customers, and it's kind of our job, in a way, to provide materials on our countertops
about the truth about manufacturers' warranties and your statutory guarantees, and I'm really
quite proud of the fact that many of our members, so if you go to an independent repairer, you'll
find on the countertop information about your consumer rights.
So, we started to use the membership as a way of pushing out the message about the difference
between a manufacturer's warranty and how your statutory consumer rights will endure,
despite the fact that the manufacturer's warranty may be completed in three or five or seven
years in the case of a brand-new car.
So, it was a real growing up for us, rather than demanding that the regulators and government
put out more and more information to support consumer choice, was us saying, well, you
know what, we've got a custom interface, too, and maybe we're part of that solution.
And so far, that's having a great deal of success.
We've printed these materials for our independent repairers, and they're on high rotation, so
we're up to the third or fourth reprint, and we've given them a kit so that they're able
to provide good information to customers immediately.
We're also providing a really interesting legal service to consumers now.
So, our members' customers, if they have a warranty rejected because they used an independent
repairer, we're able to provide a legal hotline.
And we've been doing that for a couple of years now.
It started with a very slow burn, but it's now a very well-used service.
And I think that really does show consumers that we're very confident about the quality
of our repair.
We've got good quality.
We've got highly qualified technicians.
We only use quality parts and fit-for-purpose parts because we also offer a statutory guarantee
on our work.
But consumers, I think, are becoming more aware of the hotline.
We're referring more members to it.
And I must say, the strike rate is very good.
When a consumer is armed with the right language, they know how to have that conversation at
the dealership about their warranty rights.
We're just getting, frankly, close to 100% success rate in getting a remedy for what
is a defect.
So, I think just wanted to highlight the fact that, as industry, we can also be providing
good information to consumers about what their rights are.
Thanks, Lesley.
And I must say, I've looked at your brochures and they're fantastic.
They're really plain English and it really empowers consumers as to what their rights
are.
And I think that's certainly what the Productivity Commission are thinking along those lines.
Guido, welcome.
Are you with us?
No.
We might go to Karen.
Sorry, Guido.
We'll try and sort something out for you in the meantime.
The next presenter we have is Karen Ellis.
And Karen and Dan are repairers who travel around Victoria.
They're known as Mended Australia.
But they're very passionate repairers and they visit repair cafes.
And I think you've got some really interesting stories to share about some of your repair
interactions amongst the community more generally.
Karen?
Okay.
When I received a know-of-sorts activity back in 2012, it got me thinking.
And I had the same question that Steve Wozniak, the co-founder of Apple, had in his YouTube
video posted yesterday.
Can we stop the self-repair community?
Yes, we may indeed stop us from fixing our stuff.
I knew that if repair was to have a future in local communities, my husband Danny and
I had to help make that happen along with other repair enthusiasts.
We both knew that there was no time to waste.
We had to get out in the community repairing.
Since 2015, under the banner of Mended Australia, Danny and I have volunteered at over 190 community
events on Victoria, including online sessions related to reuse, circular economy, Mended
advocates for the right to repair legislation globally, and campaigns for Australian right
to repair legislation.
As a community that mostly attends registered repair cafes, we must make it clear that it
enjoys volunteering in communities as a free entity and welcomes and promotes diversity
in community repair models.
This suggests that by only mentioning repair cafes, the unintentional effect of excluding
those repair groups that choose to develop their own identities using a different title.
Mended believes that the best way to repair can happen, and that Australia's first national
repair summit is a good place to start discussions of how best to support repair at a grassroots level.
It's at this level that some heavy lifting is being undertaken by passionate repairers
and repair advocates, helping consumers keep their useful, mostly inexpensive household
items and textiles from permaturely being down-cycled or sent to landfill.
Community repair events are amazing.
Mended has repairing and mending skills that it can share.
It's extremely motivating for our creative minds to use our skills to troubleshoot broken items.
It's the best often fixed to repair these items, and we experience the repair joy.
However, pre-community repair activities can be fraught with challenges and barriers.
Here are some of these.
Ad-hoc funding from benevolent bureaucrats.
The question, why should repair people be working for free to deliver free services?
Excessive insurance coverage.
Some brokers are reported to be refusing repair groups.
Three, liability and risk factors issues.
Four, venue hire costs.
Like men's sheds, governments have not committed to dedicated repair sheds or similar
in their waste and resource recovery plans for a circular economy.
Five, lack of volunteers.
However, mended does not mean there is a lack of expertise out there.
Myth six, about safety abound.
Some of these are submissions to the Productivity Commission.
Seven, no formal support aligns with Australian community repairers and groups.
Hopefully, an outcome of the summit will be to address this issue.
Eight, bureaucratic requirements for the repair activity.
Nine, limited access manuals, diagrams and schematics.
This issue could be addressed by right to repair legislation to ensure community repairers
are not accessing these.
Ten, items that are glued shut or hard to get into due to proprietary and hidden screws.
Again, right to repair legislation related to designing products to address this issue
could be helpful.
Eleven, the cost of testing equipment, its calibration and the training of volunteers
are expensive to fund.
Our submission to the Commission has some details on the lucrative business of pad machines
testing and compensating associated costs.
I quote from Shirley White, author of Victim to Victim.
When others tell you you can't, then they actually fear that you can, and are even more
afraid that you will.
Go away, you right to repair.
Thank you.
Thank you, Karen.
Guido, are you able to chat to us now?
Hello, can you hear me?
Hello, I can hear you.
Excellent.
Great, thank you.
A few trials and errors, but we are here.
So, good afternoon, everybody.
Yeah, my experiences with repair go back from my time with the Bower, where we had repair
cafes introduced in Australia and had our own repair services for electronics, woodwork
and bikes.
And many of the issues have already been mentioned that we were confronted with, the plant
obsolescence, the difficulty to open items for woodwork.
It's labor-intense.
Every repair is, in fact, a labor-intense task and therefore expensive.
And that's why we have been arguing for tax deductibility and deducting your expenses
for repair from your income, basically from your taxable income.
And that's the kind of input we have given to the Productivity Commission.
But I would like to focus here on some positive examples that we have overseas, but also here
in Australia.
And one of the more better-known examples is the Fairphone.
The issue here is extended producer responsibility that I would like to address, because I think
producers play an important role, can play a role, if they are with good intention joining
it with sustainability in mind.
And Fairphone is a perfect example of this.
This is a phone developed in Europe, in the Netherlands, actually, with parts that can
be replaced by the repair, by the consumer themselves.
They can replace every part from the microphone, from the camera, from the battery.
It's opening with screws like you no longer see with other phones.
So that's a perfect example of a good product that we should have more access to.
It's still not available in Australia, but in many places all over the world, it is already
around.
And we hope that it will come to this part of the world as well at some point.
It's rated by iFix with Kyle, who spoke earlier, as the best score, 10 out of 10.
It's also made by Fairtrade as a gold product, which means that all the components are
collected and resourced in a fair way.
And it is considered as one of the top sustainability products.
So there are good examples.
That's one of them.
Another example that I would like to suggest is Bosch, the electronic white goods producer.
They have introduced the blue movement.
Again, it's in Europe, only available, not yet here.
But it comes down to what was mentioned earlier, the service economy, where you actually don't
buy your product anymore, but you rent it.
And you have it serviced by them.
They come to your place to set it up.
They repair it for you.
They move it for you if you move to another place.
And you hold on for it for as long as you want.
And all services handled by them.
And if you want a new one later, they will take it back.
They can make the manufacturer more responsible for designing products that last longer, because
that's obviously in their interest to then have a product that is of better condition
and can be reused for a longer period.
Those two examples are in the electronics.
But something similar actually exists in the clothing industry.
There is, again, a European product designed for jeans.
MUD is the name, Mucked Jeans.
And they produce jeans that you, again, can lease.
And for $10 a month, you have your jeans.
And it's made with organic cotton locally produced and distributed.
And you keep it for as long as you want it.
And at the end of the time that you don't need it anymore, they take it back.
They can recycle it and use it again for jeans.
So there are those examples.
But there is actually also two examples here in Australia that I think would be worthwhile
to mention.
The one that I was introduced to in my time with the Bauer, it is Wilson's Elements.
And Edwin Wilson might be amongst the audience now.
He also registered.
And he had developed, six years ago, universal replacement parts.
Because he had analyzed and concluded that, rightly, many products after a while don't
provide spare parts anymore and makes it impossible to repair your item.
So he developed universal parts for heating elements, for nuts, for fridges and stoves,
et cetera.
And he has those items now available here in Australia and has sent them also overseas.
There's an international market for it.
Example of how you can help repairs when you have no access to parts.
And another example here in Australia that I'm introduced now to in my new job with Revolve
Recycling, where we focus on bikes, that is the Pedal Club.
And what they do is they swap bikes for kids.
Because if you're young, if you have younger kids, you every six to 12 months, they need
a new bike.
So it's not very helpful to every time have to buy a new one.
And you just rent the bike for the age of your kids for the time that you need that
bike.
$20 a month on average is what it costs you.
And when you get older, you bring it back and you rent the one for the next size up.
So that's another example of what is possible, where the consumer is helped with better services
and better quality products and where both the manufacturer and the consumer can meet
their needs.
And I would like to leave it at that.
Thank you.
Thanks, Brito.
We lost you there for a little bit visually, but I'm glad to see everybody back.
Thank you.
Look, thank you very much just for sharing your experiences and where you come into this
repair discussion.
Something I'm really interested in and something I think that the Productivity Commission has
actually picked up on is how do we collect data around repairability?
All of you, particularly Choice in the automotive industry and the repair cafe industry, we
need evidence and we need data around what are the types of products that are repeatedly
failing?
Where are the issues around product obsolescence?
How do we go about, as an Australian nation, getting great data on this?
Because it's really challenging across, we hear stories, it's very anecdotal, but we
know that there is a need to present evidence rather than anecdotal stories.
So what are your suggestions individually?
I think, Erin, I might start with you because Choice have got a really good track record
on comparability of product qualities, et cetera.
So actually, I've got some good news is that we've got some data.
Fantastic.
It's a great start.
So I know that some people will have seen the Choice submission to the Productivity
Commission initial inquiry.
We run what we call our repairability or a reliability survey every year.
We've been doing it for over 10 years.
And we speak to anywhere between 4,000 and 11,000 Choice members.
So not the average member of the public, usually people who are more informed.
They read Choice.
They engage with the issues.
We ask them what products they have and what issues they've experienced with those products
in the last 12 months.
So we've pulled that data forward.
It's in our submission.
And we've got some really interesting trends.
We know not just what products are failing more regularly, stickbacks, printers, laptops,
mobiles, but also the points of failure.
And that's a starting point.
If we want to start to rank and rate products, we know what's more likely to happen.
Even depending on the nature of the product, we've got trends with brands as well.
So we've got something to start with.
But we'd love some data, particularly around what manufacturers are doing.
So if they're able to answer questions publicly around things like what spare parts you have
easily available, how much will it cost for someone to repair something, and how long
will you hold this for, that helps us get a sense of repairability.
I think that's excellent.
That's some great ideas.
Lesley, did you have any observations?
I think you're muted.
That we have, Leanne.
Sorry.
Thanks.
I think we've got great technicians and great repairers.
And we need to be talking with them about repairability.
So we've got the issue about where the products fail.
But some products are going to require regular maintenance and repair just because of use.
And we've got a lot of expertise in our workshops.
And we're looking now at how we start to mine that, to ask about repairability.
And that meaning, do you have to move a huge component in order to get to the component
that regularly needs replacement?
That adds labour cost.
Do you need to buy a massive component instead of the small bolt or the small spring?
I just think we haven't turned our attention to it.
We've kept it very anecdotal.
And we are now looking as an industry, as I think many are, about how do we do this

Find a way to regularly engage, maybe on an annual basis, with what are the vehicles that

Because it saves the consumer in labour, time and convenience.
Thank you.
And I think another point that's been raised in these discussions, and then I'll hand it

We've all bought products probably in the belief that if you spend $250 on a toaster,

But this lack of information at the point of sale, I myself have bought external lights

So it is this very simple example of information at the point of sale about can I fix this
or not?
Anna, can you perhaps give us some questions for the panel?
Thank you.
Great, there we go.
So for Karen, do you think it is time for many disparate repair cafes and like organisations

Can you hear me?
Yes.
Yes.
Yes, absolutely.
That's what we need.
I'm getting some feedback here.
I'm sorry, I'm listening to myself.
And yes, we hope that this is what's going to come out of the repair summit that we can

repairers.
Thanks, Karen.
OK.

Yeah, it's true.

Leon, your problem with your lights would have been solved if that would have existed

Thanks, Guido.

Thanks.
Thank you.

Yes, we certainly need governments to be handing out funding, and not just the three or four

Yes, and the world doesn't have to be reinvented.

Yes, it needs to be legislated.
